source.title: Cross-Lingual Alignment for Decoder-Only Models using MoE Routers
source.authors: Lucas Bandarkar; C. Peng; A. H. Ahmed; Aditi Khandelwal; Nan-Yun Peng

record.tranche_reason: The study deliberately trains models to increase cross-lingual alignment as a method for improving multilingual performance. Its alignment results measure the effect of that imposed intervention, not whether alignment naturally rises with scale or capability.
record.gate_note: The paper measures router divergence and hidden-state alignment after alignment-loss training. It also reports downstream benchmark scores, but those assess the training method's performance rather than whether the claim's scale-related convergence occurs. Prior-work results in the related-work section are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It deliberately induces cross-lingual alignment inside a single MoE model with an auxiliary routing-KL loss during continual pre-training. It then measures alignment between languages within that same model, not between independently trained models, seeds, or modalities. It neither tests nor relies on convergence across models. The gate excludes behaviour induced on purpose, so its alignment rows fit no version. The reader's T4/uses_without_test overstates the link: the method draws on cross-lingual-transfer literature, not on the convergence claim or its originals. The study only touches the theme, by noting that language-shared middle-layer representations arise in LLMs.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also say the results give causal evidence that cross-lingual alignment improves multilingual transfer. The routing loss beat baseline CPT on average in 13 of 14 model-language pairs (one tie), with a mean gain of 0.9 points. Router-pooled alignment beat hidden-state pooling in a two-language Marco-Nano ablation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses continual pre-training with an auxiliary KL loss on mean-pooled router distributions for translated sequences; it does not reproduce a scale-based convergence measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment loss is applied to selected middle-layer ranges, which differ by model; the paper says layer selection is based on routing-divergence curves and notes prior work found router steering sensitive to exact layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Auxiliary routing-KL CPT reduced entropy-normalized JS routing divergence from English on FLORES for all four models and all seven languages. Baseline CPT changed routing only slightly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An auxiliary cross-lingual routing loss on parallel data increases within-model cross-lingual routing alignment in MoE LLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: For Qwen3-30B-A3B, the routing loss raised SoftCKA hidden-state similarity to English for Telugu, Kyrgyz, Kannada and Thai.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Aligning MoE router outputs across languages also aligns the hidden states feeding them.

fits_no_version.finding: Base-model routing-divergence curves (Fig. 6) show lower divergence in middle layers and for higher-resource languages, before any training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretrained MoE LLMs naturally share experts across languages in middle layers, more so for higher-resource languages.

record.problems: Alignment improvements are induced by the training objective and therefore do not establish natural convergence with scale or capability. Numerical values for the routing-divergence and hidden-state-alignment plots are not stated in the text. Hidden-state alignment results are shown for Qwen3-30B-A3B only. Experiments use short CPT runs on post-trained checkpoints and 200,000 samples per language.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numerical downstream benchmark rows were extracted because they assess task performance after induced alignment rather than a version's convergence measure. The benchmark tables are in Sections 5.2 and Appendix B.

untested.parts: All of it: no comparison of independently trained models across scale or capability.
All of it: no vision-language or paired image-caption data.
All of it: no seed-to-seed comparisons.
All of it: no mapping or stitching between models.
All of it: no feature or circuit recurrence across models.
All of it: no metric-sensitivity analysis of cross-model convergence. FLORES is used only as OOD eval data for the study's own intervention.
All of it: no measure of how complete natural cross-model alignment is, or what causes it.

missing.what: Base-model layer-wise routing divergence across languages, used for layer selection. This is a naturally occurring within-model cross-lingual alignment measurement and relates to no version.

record.verdict_notes: This is a within-model cross-lingual alignment study with an imposed objective. It is unrelated to cross-model representational convergence. Neither original source (PRH or Convergent Learning) is cited.

versions.untested_parts: Whether alignment among independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data rises with model size or capability.
Vision-language alignment on paired images and captions and its relation to model capability.
Convergence across random seeds, features, and shared subspaces.
Mapping or stitching representations between models, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
Recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.
Whether convergence findings weaken or disappear under alternative similarity metrics, metric settings, or inputs.
Whether naturally occurring alignment is incomplete or plateaus, or is explained by shared training data or objectives.

relation.reason: The paper discusses shared representations and cross-lingual alignment, but its within-model intervention does not test any listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The experiments deliberately induce alignment between languages within each model. They neither test nor use convergence between independently trained models as defined by the claim versions.

source_check.notes: Row states describe the study's own intervention and comparator; all rows remain linked to no claim version. For r3, Table 7 specifies auxiliary-loss layers 7–34; the caption leaves the target language unspecified, and numerical alignment values are not stated.
